o: We must simulate one Minesweeper click. If the clicked cell is a mine, mark it 'X' and stop. Otherwise, if it has adjacent mines, replace it with that count's digit. If it has zero adjacent mines, it becomes 'B' and every adjacent unrevealed ('E') cell is revealed by the same rules — a classic flood fill. In Example 1, clicking (3,0) reveals a blank region: (3,0) has no adjacent mines so it becomes 'B', and its neighbors are recursively revealed; cells adjacent to the mine at (1,2) become digits '1'. In Example 2, clicking the 'E' next to the mine simply turns it into 'X' since it was actually a mine. With m, n ≤ 50, any traversal visiting each cell once is trivially fast.
k: The click triggers either a game-over ('X'), a digit reveal, or a flood fill of blanks.
Count adjacent mines first; only recurse/expand when the count is 0 — otherwise stop at that cell.
Mark cells as revealed before pushing them to avoid revisiting and infinite loops.

a.i: Recursively reveal cells. For each cell, count mines in its 8 neighbors; if > 0 write the digit and stop, else set 'B' and recurse into all neighboring 'E' cells. Recursion depth is bounded by m*n = 2500, which is safe.
s: If board[clickr][clickc] == 'M', set it to 'X' and return.
Define dfs(r, c): if out of bounds or not 'E', return.
Count adjacent mines in the 8 directions.
If count > 0, set cell to that digit character; otherwise set 'B' and call dfs on each of the 8 neighbors.
Call dfs(clickr, clickc) and return the board.
a.t: O(m·n) — each cell is visited at most once during the flood fill.
a.sp: O(m·n) worst case for the recursion stack (e.g., an all-blank board).

a.i: Same logic but iterative: process cells from a queue instead of recursion. This avoids deep recursion stacks and is preferred in languages with small default stack sizes.
s: If the click hits a mine, set 'X' and return.
Push the click position onto a queue and mark it processed immediately.
Pop a cell; count adjacent mines.
If count > 0, write the digit; else set 'B' and push all adjacent 'E' cells after marking them 'B' to prevent duplicates.
Repeat until the queue is empty.
a.t: O(m·n) — each cell enters the queue at most once.
a.sp: O(m·n) for the queue in the worst case.

w: In an interview, DFS is the cleanest to explain; switch to BFS if recursion depth is a concern (it isn't here given m, n ≤ 50). Common pitfalls: forgetting the 4 diagonal neighbors when counting mines, recursing into already-revealed cells (causing infinite loops), and forgetting the immediate mine-click case before starting the fill. Edge cases: single-cell boards, clicking directly on a mine, and clicks on cells already surrounded by mines (digit reveal, no expansion). Follow-ups might ask for iterative solutions, handling multiple clicks, or revealing only orthogonal neighbors in a variant rule set.
